Atom GS2020 PRO MAX — instrument, model, and spectra

Working page for the instrument: description of the spectrometer and its Geant4 model, followed by measured spectra and their decomposition. The page presents three spectra in Marinelli 1 L — a Th-232 reference sample, potassium chloride (K-40), and dried blueberries (Cs-137 and K-40, the first sample with unknown activity); Ra-226 is next.

The page was prepared with the assistance of a large language model-based assistant (Claude, Anthropic) — roles, responsibilities, and data sources are detailed in the sections “About this page and its numbers” and “Sources” at the bottom of the page.

Atom GS2020 PRO MAX — a scintillation gamma-ray spectrometer with a NaI(Tl) 2×2 inch (Ø50.8×50.8 mm) crystal. Scintillation light is collected not by a photomultiplier tube, but by a silicon photomultiplier (SiPM) array at the crystal end face; the amplifier, ADC, and thermal stabilization are housed in the same Ø63 mm aluminum enclosure, with USB Type-C connectivity. The instrument assembly is Gammaspectacular (Australia); the model on the manufacturer's website is GS-MAX-2020-NAI-SIPM.

Crystal. The manufacturer of the crystal itself is not reliably known. According to the instrument manufacturer, the crystal characteristics are very close to those of the Capescint NaI-51×51 package; the latter is adopted in the model — based on the 3D model and drawing of the package manufacturer.

Bremsstrahlung is not accounted for twice. Bremsstrahlung from β-particles is generated by the deceleration of electrons in matter and is calculated by Geant4 during electron transport; internal bremsstrahlung (IB) is generated in the decay act itself, and Geant4 does not generate it. These are two sources of the same process, which are summed in the literature (review by Italiano et al., Rep. Prog. Phys. 87, 126301, 2024; for K-40 — Graham, Phys. Med. Biol. 28, 19, 1983). In the β-template of Method 2, only primary decay photons (γ and X-ray) are excluded: they are excluded from transport at the moment of creation, whereas bremsstrahlung photons generated by electrons in matter are transported and contribute to the response.

Internal bremsstrahlung in the case of K-40

What it is. In β⁻ decay 40K → 40Ca, the electron is created in the nucleus and leaves it, accelerated by the Coulomb field; simultaneously, the nuclear charge increases by one unit in a time negligible compared to the characteristic times of the atomic shell. The sudden appearance of a moving charge is accompanied by the emission of electromagnetic radiation — internal bremsstrahlung. The probability of emitting one photon per β-electron is of the order of the fine-structure constant α ≈ 1/137. The spectrum of this radiation is continuous, from zero to the β endpoint energy (for K-40 — 1311 keV). This is not the 1460.8 keV line: that line is produced by the γ transition of the daughter argon following electron capture (about 10 % of decays), not by bremsstrahlung.

How it differs from bremsstrahlung of β-particles. An electron that has already left the nucleus is decelerated in the sample, container, and housing matter and also emits a continuous spectrum; this is calculated by Geant4 during electron transport. Internal bremsstrahlung is generated in the decay act itself, does not depend on the surrounding matter, and is not simulated by Geant4 (verified in the decay source code: the products contain only the electron, antineutrino, and ion).

How it is calculated. The classical theory of Bloch and Knipp–Uhlenbeck (1936) was derived for allowed transitions and does not account for the Coulomb field of the nucleus; Lewis and Ford (1957) added the first-order Coulomb correction; Gebhardt (1968) provided the theory for any degree of forbiddenness. K-40 decays via a third unique forbidden β⁻ transition — one of the most strongly forbidden. The only known IB calculation for K-40 (Graham, 1983) was performed using the simple Bloch–Knipp–Uhlenbeck theory; no measurements of K-40 IB are found in the literature (review by Italiano et al., 2024, §4.7).

Potential contribution. According to our KUB table for K-40, the value is on the order of 9·10−3 photons per decay above 5 keV; in the fit window, this corresponds to about 2 % of the model, and the activity would be approximately 1 % lower if IB were included. For forbidden transitions, measured IB is usually higher than the KUB calculation, especially at high energies, so this estimate may be an underestimate.

Why IB is not included in the calculation for K-40. The magnitude and shape of IB for this transition are not confirmed by either measurement or a verified formula, and the measured KCl spectrum does not require IB (the fit does not improve when it is included). Therefore, IB is not included in the model pending numerical confirmation; it can be reinstated when the following conditions are met: a formula for the third unique forbidden transition, verification on a nuclide of the same class, comparison of calculations with and without IB on the measured spectrum, energy balance and normalization per decay, and a separate decision regarding electron capture.

Not accounted for or simplified. The soft region below 150 keV is not yet included in the fit. Shielding of the external background by the sample is accounted for by calculation (#GS-44, #GS-60), but below 35 keV the model remains below the measurement: the nonproportionality of NaI light yield and the lower-level discriminator (LLD) threshold are not described. The IB spectrum according to KUB is derived for allowed transitions; for K-40 (third unique forbidden) the Gebhardt (1968) theory formula has not been studied, and the shape correction and the forbidden transition matrix element are not accounted for — the magnitude and shape of IB are known only as an estimate, and its uncertainty cannot be reduced to a single number. Internal bremsstrahlung (IB) in the electron capture of K-40 (about 11 % of decays) is not added; a rough estimate without Coulomb corrections gives a negligible yield, but it is unstable (for other nuclei, experimental values are orders of magnitude higher than such a theory). The energy carried away by the IB photon is not subtracted from the β-electron — by calculation, about 0.01–0.03 % of the model. Bremsstrahlung of β-particles in matter is reproduced by Geant4 with an accuracy of the order of 10–50 % (Pandola et al., 2015), meaning its contribution to activity is known only to within fractions of a percent — of the same order as the total internal bremsstrahlung contribution. The agreement of Method 1 and Method 2 on KCl is a check of implementation consistency, not of the physical model: both use the same Geant4, the same geometry, and the same expected activity.

The moisture content of the sample is unknown: the expected activity is given for dry KCl, and moisture reduces it.

KCl: spectrum {{date_meas}}, live time {{tlive}}, real time {{treal}}; Marinelli+water background — live time {{kp_bg_live}}. The measurement was performed in two parts (41.5 h and 46.8 h) with a 2.4 h pause; after the pause, the instrument gain increased slightly, and the K-40 peak in the second part was located 2.2 keV higher. Therefore, the second part was shifted to the scale of the first part before summation (based on the shape calibration of each part); a simple sum would have mixed the two peak positions and distorted the scale near the threshold.

Why χ²/ν is large. The fit criterion accounts for the statistical noise of the Geant4 template itself; until 09.10.2026 this noise was calculated assuming the template was not broadened, and after broadening it was overestimated by hundreds of times — χ²/ν appeared close to one despite a visible discrepancy. Now the noise is calculated accurately, and the discrepancy is visible: the peak width of the 1460.8 keV line is the same in the model and in the measurement (approximately 80 keV), but the shape of the K-40 template is different — in the model the full-energy peak is higher than measured, while the 150–600 keV region is lower. A single amplitude cannot describe both parts of the spectrum simultaneously, therefore the activity depends on the fit weights. The cause of the shape is being investigated (backscatter from the surroundings, response near the Compton edge, housing materials). The density, composition, and volume of the sample do not explain the discrepancy: the template is calculated in the geometry of the KCl sample itself, and these are already accounted for. Since 10.10.2026 the energy scale of the spectrum is smooth: the previous piecewise-linear scale produced steps in the template (245 and 580 keV) and distorted the peak widths in the plot; on the smooth scale the excess in the 250–650 keV range disappeared, while the 1460.8 keV peak in the model remains approximately 3 % narrower than the measured one — the measured peak has broader wings. This sample serves as an independent check of the detector data set (efficiency curve, response matrix, peak width — based on the thorium reference spectrum, density and sample volume corrections); the data set and the verification report are published in the repository geant4-detector-models, dataset.

Bremsstrahlung is not accounted for twice. Bremsstrahlung from β-particles is generated by the deceleration of electrons in matter and is calculated by Geant4 during electron transport; internal bremsstrahlung (IB) is generated in the decay act itself, and Geant4 does not generate it. These are two sources of the same process, which are summed in the literature (review by Italiano et al., Rep. Prog. Phys. 87, 126301, 2024; for K-40 — Graham, Phys. Med. Biol. 28, 19, 1983). In the β-template of Method 2, only primary decay photons (γ and X-ray) are excluded: they are excluded from transport at the moment of creation, whereas bremsstrahlung photons generated by electrons in matter are transported and contribute to the response.

Internal bremsstrahlung in the case of K-40

What it is. In β⁻ decay 40K → 40Ca, the electron is created in the nucleus and leaves it, accelerated by the Coulomb field; simultaneously, the nuclear charge increases by one unit in a time negligible compared to the characteristic times of the atomic shell. The sudden appearance of a moving charge is accompanied by the emission of electromagnetic radiation — internal bremsstrahlung. The probability of emitting one photon per β-electron is of the order of the fine-structure constant α ≈ 1/137. The spectrum of this radiation is continuous, from zero to the β endpoint energy (for K-40 — 1311 keV). This is not the 1460.8 keV line: that line is produced by the γ transition of the daughter argon following electron capture (about 10 % of decays), not by bremsstrahlung.

How it differs from bremsstrahlung of β-particles. An electron that has already left the nucleus is decelerated in the sample, container, and housing materials and also emits a continuous spectrum; this is calculated by Geant4 during electron transport. Internal bremsstrahlung is generated in the decay act itself, is independent of the surrounding material, and is not simulated by Geant4 (verified in the decay source code: the products contain only the electron, antineutrino, and ion).

How it is calculated. The classical theory of Bloch and Knipp–Uhlenbeck (1936) was derived for allowed transitions and does not account for the Coulomb field of the nucleus; Lewis and Ford (1957) added the first-order Coulomb correction; Gebhardt (1968) provided the theory for any degree of forbiddenness. K-40 decays via a third unique forbidden β⁻ transition — one of the most strongly forbidden. The only known IB calculation for K-40 (Graham, 1983) was performed using the simple Bloch–Knipp–Uhlenbeck theory; no measurements of K-40 IB are reported in the literature (review by Italiano et al., 2024, §4.7).

Estimate of the possible contribution. According to our KUB table, for K-40 it is on the order of 9·10−3 photons per decay above 5 keV; in the fit window this corresponds to about 2 % of the model, and the activity would be approximately 1 % lower if IB were included. For forbidden transitions, measured IB is usually higher than the KUB calculation, especially at high energies, so this estimate may be an underestimate.

Why IB is not included in the calculation for K-40. The magnitude and shape of IB for this transition are confirmed neither by measurement nor by a validated formula, and the measured KCl spectrum does not require IB (the fit does not improve when it is included). Therefore, IB is not included in the model pending numerical confirmation; it can be reinstated when the following conditions are met: a formula for the third unique forbidden transition, verification on a nuclide of the same class, comparison of calculations with and without IB on the measured spectrum, energy balance and normalization per decay, and a separate decision regarding electron capture.

Not accounted for or simplified. The soft region below 150 keV is not yet included in the fit. Shielding of the external background by the sample is accounted for by calculation (#GS-44, #GS-60), but below 35 keV the model remains below the measurement: the nonproportionality of NaI light yield and the lower-level discriminator (LLD) threshold are not described. The IB spectrum according to KUB is derived for allowed transitions; for K-40 (third unique forbidden) the Gebhardt (1968) theory formula has not been studied, and the shape correction and the forbidden transition matrix element are not accounted for — the magnitude and shape of IB are known only as an estimate, and its uncertainty cannot be reduced to a single number. Internal bremsstrahlung (IB) during electron capture of K-40 (about 11 % of decays) is not added; a rough estimate without Coulomb corrections gives a negligible emission probability, but it is unstable (for other nuclei, experimental values are orders of magnitude higher than such a theory). The energy carried away by the IB photon is not subtracted from the β-electron — according to the calculation, about 0.01–0.03 % of the model. Bremsstrahlung of β-particles in matter is reproduced by Geant4 with an accuracy of the order of 10–50 % (Pandola et al., 2015), meaning its contribution to activity is known only to within fractions of a percent — of the same order as the total internal bremsstrahlung contribution. The agreement of Method 1 and Method 2 on KCl is a check of implementation consistency, not of the physical model: both use the same Geant4, the same geometry, and the same expected activity.

The measurement was performed in two parts (41.5 h and 46.8 h) with a 2.4 h pause; after the pause, the instrument gain increased slightly, and the K-40 peak in the second part was located 2.2 keV higher. Therefore, the second part was shifted to the scale of the first part before summation (based on the shape calibration of each part); a simple sum would have mixed the two peak positions and distorted the scale near the threshold.

Why χ²/ν is large. The fit criterion accounts for the statistical noise of the Geant4 template itself; until 09.10.2026 this noise was calculated assuming the template was not broadened, and after broadening it was overestimated by hundreds of times — χ²/ν appeared close to one despite a visible discrepancy. Now the noise is calculated accurately, and the discrepancy is visible: the peak width of the 1460.8 keV line is the same in the model and in the measurement (about 80 keV), but the shape of the K-40 template is different — in the model the full-energy peak is higher than measured, while the 150–600 keV region is lower. A single amplitude cannot describe both parts of the spectrum simultaneously, so the activity depends on the fit weights. The cause of the shape is being investigated (backscatter from the surroundings, response near the Compton edge, housing materials). The sample density, composition, and volume do not explain the discrepancy: the template is calculated in the geometry of the KCl sample itself, and these are already accounted for. Since 10.10.2026, the spectrum energy scale is smooth: the previous piecewise-linear scale produced steps in the template (245 and 580 keV) and distorted the peak widths in the plot; on the smooth scale, the excess in the 250–650 keV range disappeared, while the 1460.8 keV peak in the model remains approximately 3 % narrower than the measured one — the measured peak has broader wings. This sample serves as an independent check of the detector data set (efficiency curve, response matrix, peak width — based on the thorium reference spectrum, sample density and volume correction); the data set and the verification report are published in the repository geant4-detector-models, dataset.

External and internal bremsstrahlung: what is accounted for. External bremsstrahlung of β-particles is generated when electrons are decelerated in matter and is calculated by Geant4 during electron transport; internal bremsstrahlung (IB) is generated in the decay act itself, and Geant4 does not generate it. These are two contributions of the same physical process, which are summed in the literature (review Italiano et al., Rep. Prog. Phys. 87, 126301, 2024; for K-40 — Graham, Phys. Med. Biol. 28, 19, 1983). In the β-template of Method 2, only primary decay photons (γ and X-rays) are excluded: they are removed from transport at the moment of birth, whereas bremsstrahlung photons generated by electrons in matter are transported and included in the response.

Internal bremsstrahlung using K-40 as an example

What it is. In β⁻ decay 40K → 40Ca, the electron is born in the nucleus and leaves it, decelerating in the Coulomb field of the nucleus; simultaneously, the nuclear charge increases by one unit in a time negligible compared to the characteristic times of the atomic shell. The sudden appearance of a moving charge is accompanied by the emission of electromagnetic radiation — internal bremsstrahlung. The probability of emitting one photon per β-electron is of the order of magnitude given by the fine-structure constant α ≈ 1/137. The spectrum of this radiation is continuous, from zero to the β endpoint energy (for K-40 — 1311 keV). This is not the 1460.8 keV line: it is produced by the γ transition of the daughter argon after electron capture (about 10.7 % of decays), not by bremsstrahlung.

How it differs from bremsstrahlung of β-particles. An electron that has already left the nucleus is decelerated in the matter of the sample, container, and housing and also emits a continuous spectrum; this is calculated by Geant4 during electron transport. Internal bremsstrahlung is generated in the decay act itself, does not depend on the surrounding matter, and Geant4 does not generate it (verified in the source code of the decay model: the products are only the electron, antineutrino, and ion).

How it is calculated. The classical Knipp–Uhlenbeck–Bloch (KUB, 1936) theory is derived for allowed transitions and does not account for the Coulomb field of the nucleus; Lewis and Ford (1957) added the first-order Coulomb correction; Gebhardt (1968) provided the theory for any degree of forbiddenness. K-40 decays via a third unique forbidden β⁻ transition — one of the most strongly forbidden. The only known calculation of IB for K-40 (Graham, 1983) was performed using the simple KUB theory; no measurements of K-40 IB are found in the literature (review Italiano et al., 2024, §4.7).

Estimation of the possible contribution. According to the KUB spectrum table calculated for K-40, the internal bremsstrahlung (IB) yield is on the order of 9·10−3 photons per decay above 5 keV; within the fit window, this corresponds to approximately 2 % of the model, and the activity would be approximately 1 % lower if IB were included. For forbidden transitions, the measured IB is typically higher than the KUB calculation, particularly at high energies; therefore, this estimate may be an underestimate.

Why IB is not included in the calculation for K-40. The magnitude and shape of the IB for this transition are not confirmed by either measurement or a validated formula, and no evidence of an IB contribution was found in the measured KCl spectrum (the fit does not improve when IB is included). Consequently, IB is excluded from the model pending numerical confirmation. It may be reinstated once the following conditions are met: a formula for the third unique forbidden transition, verification on a nuclide of the same class, comparison of calculations with and without IB against the measured spectrum, energy balance and normalization per decay, and a separate determination for electron capture.

Not accounted for or simplified. The low-energy region below 150 keV is not included in the fit. Shielding of the external background by the sample is accounted for in the calculation, but below 35 keV the model remains lower than the measurement: the nonproportionality of the NaI(Tl) light yield and the lower-level discriminator (LLD) threshold are not described. The KUB IB spectrum is derived for allowed transitions; for K-40 (third unique forbidden), the Gebhardt (1968) theoretical formula is not used in the calculation, and the shape correction and the forbidden matrix element are not accounted for — the magnitude and shape of the IB are known only as an estimate, and its uncertainty cannot be reduced to a single number. Internal bremsstrahlung from electron capture in K-40 (approximately 10.7 % of decays) is not added; an approximate estimate without Coulomb corrections yields a negligible yield, but it is unstable (for other nuclei, experimental values exceed such theoretical calculations by several times). The energy carried away by the IB photon is not subtracted from the β-electron — according to the calculation, this is approximately 0.01–0.03 % of the model. External bremsstrahlung of β-particles in matter is reproduced by Geant4 with an accuracy of the order of 10–50 % (Pandola et al., 2015), meaning the uncertainty in its contribution to the activity is on the order of fractions of a percent — the same order of magnitude as the total contribution of internal bremsstrahlung. The agreement between Method 1 and Method 2 on KCl is a check of implementation consistency, not of the physical model: both use the same Geant4, the same geometry, and the same expected activity.

The laboratory background was recorded without the beaker and is subtracted using a fixed coefficient — the ratio of live times. The beaker with the sample shields the instrument from the background, therefore subtracting the entire background spectrum leads to over-subtraction. The “Marinelli+water” option uses a second measurement — the same beaker with distilled water instead of thorium, calibrated with the same own energy scale (reference lines of this spectrum) and the same live time ratio. Cascade pairs of γ-quanta from a single decay, registered together, contribute at the sum energy; pairs with a confirmed common decay scheme level are accounted for. External and internal bremsstrahlung: what is accounted for. External bremsstrahlung of β particles is generated when electrons are decelerated in matter and is calculated by Geant4 during electron transport; internal bremsstrahlung (IB) is generated in the decay act itself, and Geant4 does not generate it. These are two contributions of the same physical process, which are summed in the literature (review Italiano et al., Rep. Prog. Phys. 87, 126301, 2024; for K-40 — Graham, Phys. Med. Biol. 28, 19, 1983). In the β template of Method 2, only primary decay photons (γ and X-rays) are excluded: they are removed from transport at the moment of birth, while bremsstrahlung photons generated by electrons in matter are transported and included in the response.

Internal bremsstrahlung using K-40 as an example

What it is. In β⁻ decay 40K → 40Ca, the electron is born in the nucleus and leaves it, decelerating in the Coulomb field of the nucleus; simultaneously, the nuclear charge increases by one unit in a time negligible compared to the characteristic times of the atomic shell. The sudden appearance of a moving charge is accompanied by the emission of electromagnetic radiation — internal bremsstrahlung. The probability of emitting one photon per β electron is of the order of the fine-structure constant α ≈ 1/137. The spectrum of this radiation is continuous, from zero to the β endpoint energy (for K-40 — 1311 keV). This is not the 1460.8 keV line: it is produced by the γ transition of the daughter argon after electron capture (about 10.7 % of decays), not by bremsstrahlung.

How it differs from β-particle bremsstrahlung. An electron that has already left the nucleus is decelerated in the sample, beaker, and housing matter and also emits a continuous spectrum; this is calculated by Geant4 during electron transport. Internal bremsstrahlung is generated in the decay act itself, does not depend on the surrounding matter, and Geant4 does not generate it (verified in the decay model source code: products include only the electron, antineutrino, and ion).

How it is calculated. The classical Knipp–Uhlenbeck–Bloch (KUB, 1936) theory is derived for allowed transitions and does not account for the nuclear Coulomb field; Lewis and Ford (1957) added the first-order Coulomb correction; Gebhardt (1968) provided the theory for any degree of forbiddenness. K-40 decays via a third-forbidden unique β⁻ transition — one of the most strongly forbidden. The only known internal bremsstrahlung (IB) calculation for K-40 (Graham, 1983) was performed using the simple KUB theory; no measurements of K-40 IB are reported in the literature (review by Italiano et al., 2024, §4.7).

Estimate of the possible contribution. According to the KUB spectrum table calculated for K-40, the IB yield is on the order of 9·10−3 photons per decay above 5 keV; in the fit window, this corresponds to about 2 % of the model, and the activity would be approximately 1 % lower if IB were included. For forbidden transitions, the measured IB is typically higher than the KUB calculation, especially at high energies, so this estimate may be an underestimate.

Why IB is not included in the calculation for K-40. The magnitude and shape of the IB for this transition are confirmed neither by measurement nor by a validated formula, and no signs of an IB contribution were detected in the measured KCl spectrum (the fit does not improve when IB is included). Therefore, IB is not included in the model pending numerical confirmation; it can be reinstated when the following conditions are met: a formula for the third-forbidden unique transition, validation on a nuclide of the same class, comparison of calculations with and without IB on the measured spectrum, energy balance and normalization per decay, and a separate decision regarding electron capture.

Not accounted for or simplified. The low-energy region below 150 keV is not included in the fit. Shielding of the external background by the sample is accounted for in the calculation, but below 35 keV the model remains lower than the measurement: the scintillation light-yield nonproportionality of NaI(Tl) and the lower-level discriminator (LLD) threshold are not described. The KUB IB spectrum is derived for allowed transitions; for K-40 (third-forbidden unique transition), the formula from Gebhardt's theory (1968) is not used in the calculation, and the shape correction and forbidden matrix element are not accounted for — the magnitude and shape of the IB are known only as an estimate, and its uncertainty cannot be reduced to a single number. Internal bremsstrahlung from electron capture in K-40 (about 10.7 % of decays) is not added; an approximate estimate without Coulomb corrections gives a negligible yield, but it is unstable (for other nuclei, experiments exceed such theoretical calculations by several times). The energy carried away by the IB photon is not subtracted from the β electron — according to the calculation, this is about 0.01–0.03 % of the model. External bremsstrahlung of β particles in matter is reproduced by Geant4 with an accuracy of the order of 10–50 % (Pandola et al., 2015), meaning the uncertainty of its contribution to the activity is a fraction of a percent — of the same order as the total internal bremsstrahlung contribution. The agreement between Method 1 and Method 2 on KCl is a check of implementation consistency, not of the physical model: both use the same Geant4, the same geometry, and the same expected activity.

The decay-chain template is the sum of the Monte Carlo full-decay templates of the chain members ({{nuclide_list}}); each member is a separate Geant4 calculation for an ion source of its nuclide in the beaker volume with a decay-chain limitation (the nucleusLimits parameter of the Geant4 package), so that adjacent members do not contribute. The number of simulated decays of a member is proportional to its branching ({{tpl_decays}}), so the sum of the unprocessed histograms gives the decay-chain template in equilibrium. Geant4 does not generate internal bremsstrahlung (IB), and it is not included in the calculation until numerically confirmed. The template is broadened by the FWHM(E) function and fitted with a single amplitude by two criteria: A2 — weighted least-squares fit to the net spectrum without truncation, where the channel weight accounts for the measurement variance and the template variance; E1 — minimum total variation of the normalized shapes at equality of the model and net sums. The A2 uncertainty is multiplied by the Birge ratio correction √(χ²/ν) when χ²/ν is greater than one.

Method 2: full-energy-peak (FEP) efficiency function × line library

The FEP efficiency function is the full-energy peak efficiency for monoenergetic lines from Geant4 in the sample geometry. For each library energy and each sum-peak energy, a direct Geant4 calculation was performed for a monoenergetic volume source in the beaker; its full energy-deposition spectrum, broadened by the same function, is multiplied by the line emission probability and the member branching. To each member with its weight, a β component is added — an ion decay calculation in which the primary decay photons are excluded from transport at birth, while electrons are fully transported (their bremsstrahlung in the sample and beaker). Internal bremsstrahlung (IB) is not included in the calculation. The decay-chain column is the sum over the members, and the node variance is the sum of the squared weights. The fit is performed with a single amplitude, as in Method 1.

Background and the “background” switch

The laboratory background was recorded without the beaker and is subtracted with a fixed coefficient — the ratio of live times. The beaker with the sample shields the instrument from the background, so subtracting the entire background spectrum leads to over-subtraction. The “Marinelli+water” option uses a second measurement — the same beaker with distilled water instead of thorium, calibrated with the same own energy calibration (reference lines of this spectrum) and the same live-time ratio. This is a direct measurement of shielding by water; the difference between the sample and water is accounted for by the calculated r(E) correction (Geant4, external isotropic field, separate assembly for each sample). The live time of the measurement is shorter than that of the laboratory background.

True coincidence summing

Cascade pairs of γ rays from a single decay, registered together, contribute at the sum energy; pairs with a confirmed common decay-scheme level are accounted for. X-ray+γ pairs are not accounted for in Method 2. Angular correlation of the cascade is not accounted for in any method. In Method 1, summing is automatically accounted for in the full-decay templates.

Common to both methods

The FWHM(E) function; the background and its option; the energy scale; the geometry of the instrument, beaker, and sample density — one model for all calculations.

External and internal bremsstrahlung: what is accounted for. External bremsstrahlung from β particles is generated when electrons are decelerated in matter and is calculated by Geant4 during electron transport; internal bremsstrahlung (IB) is generated in the decay act itself, and Geant4 does not generate it. These are two contributions of a single physical process, which are summed in the literature (review by Italiano et al., Rep. Prog. Phys. 87, 126301, 2024; for K-40 — Graham, Phys. Med. Biol. 28, 19, 1983). In the β template of Method 2, only primary decay photons (γ rays and characteristic X-rays) are excluded: they are removed from transport at the moment of creation, whereas bremsstrahlung photons generated by electrons in matter are transported and included in the response.

Internal bremsstrahlung in the case of K-40

Definition. In β⁻ decay 40K → 40Ca, the electron is created in the nucleus and leaves it, decelerating in the Coulomb field of the nucleus; simultaneously, the nuclear charge increases by one unit in a time negligible compared to the characteristic times of the atomic shell. The sudden appearance of a moving charge is accompanied by the emission of electromagnetic radiation — internal bremsstrahlung. The probability of emitting one photon per β electron is of the order of the fine-structure constant α ≈ 1/137. The spectrum of this radiation is continuous, from zero to the β endpoint energy (for K-40 — 1311 keV). This is not the 1460.8 keV line: it is produced by the γ transition of the daughter argon following electron capture (about 10.4 % of decays: according to LNHB-DDEP 2025, 10.34 % to the 1460.8 keV level and 0.10 % to the ground state), and not by bremsstrahlung.

Difference from external bremsstrahlung of β particles. An electron that has already left the nucleus is decelerated in the sample, beaker, and housing matter and also emits a continuous spectrum; this is calculated by Geant4 during electron transport. Internal bremsstrahlung is generated in the decay act itself, does not depend on the surrounding matter, and is not generated by Geant4 (verified in the decay model source code: the products are only the electron, antineutrino, and ion).

Calculation methods. The classical Knipp–Uhlenbeck–Bloch (KUB, 1936) theory was derived for allowed transitions and does not account for the Coulomb field of the nucleus; Lewis and Ford (1957) added the first-order Coulomb correction; Gebhardt (1968) provided the theory for any degree of forbiddenness. K-40 decays via a third-forbidden unique transition — one of the most strongly forbidden. The only known IB calculation for K-40 (Graham, 1983) was performed using the simple KUB theory; no measurements of K-40 IB are found in the literature (review by Italiano et al., 2024, §4.7).

Estimate of the possible contribution. According to the KUB spectrum table calculated for K-40, the contribution is on the order of 9·10−3 photons per decay above 5 keV; in the fit window this is about 2 % of the model, and the activity would be approximately 1 % lower if IB were included. For forbidden transitions, measured IB is usually higher than the KUB calculation, especially at high energies, so this estimate may be an underestimate.

Why IB is not included in the calculation for K-40. The magnitude and shape of IB for this transition are confirmed neither by measurement nor by a verified formula, and no signs of an IB contribution are observed in the measured KCl spectrum (the fit does not improve when it is included). Therefore, IB is not included in the model until numerical confirmation is obtained; it can be reinstated when the following conditions are met: a formula for the third-forbidden unique transition, verification on a nuclide of the same class, comparison of calculations with and without IB on the measured spectrum, energy balance and normalization per decay, and a separate decision regarding electron capture.

External and internal bremsstrahlung: what is accounted for. External bremsstrahlung from β particles is generated when electrons are decelerated in matter and is calculated by Geant4 during electron transport; internal bremsstrahlung (IB) is generated in the decay act itself, and Geant4 does not generate it. These are two contributions of a single physical process, which are summed in the literature (review by Italiano et al., Rep. Prog. Phys. 87, 126301, 2024; for K-40 — Graham, Phys. Med. Biol. 28, 19, 1983). In the β template of Method 2, only primary decay photons (γ rays and characteristic X-rays) are removed: they are excluded from transport at the moment of creation, whereas bremsstrahlung photons generated by electrons in matter are transported and included in the response.

Internal bremsstrahlung in the case of K-40

Definition. In β⁻ decay 40K → 40Ca, the electron is created in the nucleus and leaves it, decelerating in the Coulomb field of the nucleus; simultaneously, the nuclear charge increases by one unit over a time negligible compared with the characteristic times of the atomic shell. The sudden appearance of a moving charge is accompanied by the emission of electromagnetic radiation — internal bremsstrahlung. The probability of emitting one photon per β electron is of the order of the fine-structure constant α ≈ 1/137. The spectrum of this radiation is continuous, from zero to the β endpoint energy (for K-40 — 1311 keV). This is not the 1460.8 keV line: that line is produced by the γ transition of the daughter argon following electron capture (about 10.4 % of decays: according to LNHB-DDEP 2025, 10.34 % to the 1460.8 keV level and 0.10 % to the ground state), not by bremsstrahlung.

Difference from external bremsstrahlung of β particles. An electron that has already left the nucleus is decelerated in the sample, beaker, and housing matter and also emits a continuous spectrum; this is calculated by Geant4 during electron transport. Internal bremsstrahlung is generated in the decay act itself, does not depend on the surrounding matter, and is not generated by Geant4 (verified in the decay model source code: the products are only the electron, antineutrino, and ion).

Calculation methods. The classical Knipp–Uhlenbeck–Bloch (KUB, 1936) theory was derived for allowed transitions and does not account for the Coulomb field of the nucleus; later, a first-order Coulomb correction and a theory for any degree of forbiddenness were added. K-40 decays via a third-forbidden unique transition — one of the most strongly forbidden. The only known IB calculation for K-40 (Graham, 1983) was performed using the simple KUB theory; no measurements of K-40 IB are found in the literature (review by Italiano et al., 2024, §4.7).

Estimate of the possible contribution. According to the KUB spectrum table calculated for K-40, the contribution is on the order of 9·10−3 photons per decay above 5 keV; in the fit window this is about 2 % of the model, and the activity would be approximately 1 % lower if IB were included. For forbidden transitions, measured IB is usually higher than the KUB calculation, especially at high energies, so this estimate may be an underestimate.

Why IB is not included in the calculation for K-40. The magnitude and shape of IB for this transition are confirmed neither by measurement nor by a verified formula, and no signs of an IB contribution are observed in the measured KCl spectrum (the fit does not improve when it is included). Therefore, IB is not included in the model until its contribution is confirmed by measurement or a verified formula; it can be reinstated when the following conditions are met: a formula for the third-forbidden unique transition, verification on a nuclide of the same class, comparison of calculations with and without IB on the measured spectrum, energy balance and normalization per decay, and a separate decision regarding electron capture.

The energy carried away by the IB photon is not subtracted from the β electron — according to the calculation, about 0.01–0.03 % of the model. External bremsstrahlung of β particles in matter is reproduced by Geant4 with an accuracy of the order of 10–50 % (Pandola et al., 2015), that is, the uncertainty of its contribution to the activity is a fraction of a percent — less than the possible contribution of internal bremsstrahlung (about 1 % in activity). The expected activity is calculated from the mass, without certification: mass × potassium fraction in KCl × K-40 abundance × ln2/T½. Its uncertainty {{aksp_unc}} comprises the uncertainties of the K-40 abundance, the half-life, and the reagent purity tolerance; the balance error is unknown and not included. Geant4 does not generate internal bremsstrahlung from β decay; it is not included in the K-40 calculation (a KUB spectrum-based estimate would reduce the activity by approximately 1 %, but this is not confirmed by measurement). The γ-ray emission probability of K-40 is adopted from LNHB-DDEP 2025 ({{k40_ig_lnhb}} %); in ENSDF it is 10.66 %.

The Marinelli beaker + water background was measured for a live time of {{kp_bg_live}}. The KCl sample spectrum was measured in two runs (41.5 h and 46.8 h) with a 2.4 h pause; after the pause, the K-40 peak in the second part was located 2.2 keV higher (apparently due to a slight increase in instrument gain). Therefore, the second part was shifted to the scale of the first part (based on the peak positions of each part) before summing; a simple sum would result in the superposition of two peak positions and distort the scale near the threshold.

Reasons for the high χ²/ν value. The fit criterion accounts for the statistical noise of the Geant4 template itself. The noise is accounted for exactly (including template broadening), so the discrepancy between the model and the measurement is visible in the χ²/ν value. The FWHM of the 1460.8 keV peak in the model ({{kp_fw_k40_conv}}) and in the measurement ({{kp_fw_own}}) agrees within uncertainty, but the shape of the K-40 template differs — in the model, the full-energy peak is higher than the measured one, while the 150–600 keV region is lower. A single amplitude cannot describe both parts of the spectrum simultaneously, so the activity depends on the fit weights. The cause of the shape difference is not established (considered: NaI(Tl) scintillation light-yield nonproportionality, backscatter from the surroundings, housing materials). The density, composition, and volume of the sample do not apparently explain the discrepancy: the template is calculated in the geometry of the KCl sample itself, and these are included (assuming their values are correct; the sample moisture content is unknown). The energy scale of the spectrum is a smooth polynomial: a piecewise-linear scale caused breaks in the template shape (245 and 580 keV) and distorted the peak widths in the plot; on the smooth scale, the excess in the 250–650 keV range disappeared, but a shape difference remains in the wing region of the 1460.8 keV peak: the wings of the measured peak are wider than in the model (χ²/ν of the peak shape after accounting for gain spread — {{k40_shape}}). This sample serves as an independent check of the detector data set. The data set includes the efficiency curve and the response matrix (Geant4 calculation), the peak width (from the thorium reference spectrum), and the correction for sample density and volume; the data set and the verification report are available in the repository geant4-detector-models, dataset.
